subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Elizabeth found out on a bus ride back from the town market. Her brother Yash, who everyone thought was still working at the tile shop, had lost the job in spring and taken a loan from a local lender to keep up the pretence. Now the lender's man had begun calling at the house. Their parents thought the calls were for the shop. That evening, at the tea stall near the bus stand, she told only Aunt Mala, the retired schoolteacher, who listened without gasping. Later Elizabeth sat down with Yash. “I won't say it behind your back,” she said. “But they need to hear it before the man comes again. You tell them, and I sit beside you.”

qa.q: What had Yash lost in spring?
qa.a: Yash had lost the job at the tile shop in spring.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth worry about and want when deciding who should know?
qa.a: Elizabeth was weighing Yash's privacy against the parents' right to know before the lender's man came again. She also did not want to use the secret against him.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make about telling the parents?
qa.a: She asked Yash to tell them himself and offered to sit beside him, instead of speaking behind his back.

qa.q: How might Yash feel when Elizabeth says, “I sit beside you”?
qa.a: Yash may feel relieved that he is not left alone with it, though probably still ashamed, since he had kept up the pretence for months.

grounding: An adult who learns a hard family truth weighs privacy against safety, asks a trusted person for support and does not use the secret as a weapon.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Selin had read the letter twice before she folded it back into her late grandmother's box. It said her mother had given a baby up for adoption years before Selin was born. Nobody had ever spoken of it. That night in the flat above the bakery, Selin's father was watching a match, and her mother was on the phone with a cousin. Selin did not say a word. On Sunday she met Abebe, an old family friend who had known her mother since school, at the park. “Part of me wants to tell Papa tonight,” Selin said. “But it's her story. Maybe she should first hear from me that I know.” Abebe nodded. “Who else knows is hers to decide. Ask her gently, alone, and don't carry it as a weapon.” Selin nodded slowly.

qa.q: What did the letter in Selin's grandmother's box say?
qa.a: It said her mother had given a baby up for adoption years before Selin was born.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling when she stayed silent that night in the flat?
qa.a: Selin was probably shaken and protective of her mother, so she kept the letter to herself until she could think it through.

qa.q: What could Selin do next after the talk with Abebe?
qa.a: Selin could ask her mother gently, when they are alone, and let her mother decide who else should know.

qa.q: How might Selin's mother feel if she found out that Selin knew?
qa.a: Selin's mother might feel exposed and worried at first, so speaking gently and privately, not in front of the family, would matter to her.

grounding: An adult who learns a hard family truth weighs privacy and fairness, seeks a trusted person's advice and decides not to use the secret as a weapon.
